reference.source: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics / Tachdjian's Paediatric Orthopaedics
clinicalPearls: The most common single form of arthrogryposis multiplex congenita, characterised by symmetrical involvement of all four limbs with severe contractures
Classic posture is internally rotated and adducted shoulders, extended elbows, flexed wrists, and rigid clubfeet, with the arms often held straight and pronated ('waiter's tip'-like)
A midline facial capillary haemangioma (naevus flammeus) over the forehead is a frequent and helpful clue
Muscle is replaced by fibrous and fatty tissue (the name means 'no muscle growth'), giving a cylindrical, featureless limb
It is essentially sporadic, with a negligible recurrence risk, which is central to family counselling
Intellect is normal and, crucially, children often become functionally independent with intensive physiotherapy and surgery
Early aggressive physiotherapy, serial casting, splinting and staged orthopaedic surgery markedly improve function
reference.pathophysiology: Amyoplasia is a sporadic condition thought to result from an in-utero insult to the developing anterior horn cells or to muscle, possibly related to a vascular or hypoxic event or to prolonged foetal immobility. The loss of functioning muscle, which becomes replaced by fibrofatty tissue, leads to profound foetal akinesia during limb morphogenesis. The immobility permits periarticular connective tissue to fibrose and joints to fixate symmetrically, producing the characteristic rigid contractures. Because it is not a single-gene disorder, it does not follow Mendelian inheritance and recurrence within a family is rare.
additionalDifferentials: Distal arthrogryposis syndromes with predominantly hand and foot involvement
Neurogenic arthrogryposis from spinal cord or anterior horn cell disease
Congenital myopathies and congenital muscular dystrophies
additionalInvestigations: Clinical recognition of the symmetrical limb pattern and midline facial haemangioma
Plain radiographs of the limbs and spine to characterise deformity and exclude dislocation
Muscle imaging or biopsy showing fibrofatty replacement when the diagnosis is uncertain
Electromyography and nerve conduction studies to help distinguish myopathic from neurogenic causes
Genetic testing to exclude specific syndromic or single-gene causes
Assessment of feeding, respiratory function and hips for associated dislocation
redFlags: Hip dislocation or knee deformity limiting future mobility
Fractures sustained during birth or manipulation of rigid limbs
reference.prognosis: With intensive rehabilitation and staged surgery many children achieve good functional independence and ambulation; intellect and lifespan are normal, though residual deformity, reduced strength and the need for repeated orthopaedic intervention are common.
pitfalls: Giving an inflated recurrence risk by not recognising the sporadic nature of amyoplasia
Being unduly pessimistic about function, when many children do very well with therapy
Manipulating rigid limbs forcefully and causing fractures
Overlooking hip dislocation or scoliosis on follow-up
references: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
management: Begin intensive physiotherapy early with stretching and serial casting to reduce the fixed joint contractures
Correct residual deformity and rigid clubfeet with staged orthopaedic surgery to improve limb position and function
Provide orthoses and assistive devices to support standing, walking and upper-limb use
Use occupational therapy to build independence in daily activities, exploiting the normal intellect
Assess and manage associated problems including feeding difficulty, respiratory function and hip dislocation
Coordinate care across clinical genetics, orthopaedics and rehabilitation medicine
Reassure the family through genetic counselling that the condition is sporadic with a negligible recurrence risk
